q: The title ' Devanam Priya ' was given to:
explanation: Devanampriya ('beloved of the gods') was Ashoka's title in his edicts; Samudragupta, Kanishka and Harsha did not use it.

notes.text: - **Usual title:** **Devanampiya Piyadasi** – Devanampiya (Devanampriya) = "**Beloved of the Gods**"; Piyadasi (**Priyadarshi**) = "of pleasing appearance" (IAS 1995; MPPSC 2015; APPSC G1) – not Chakravarti, Dharmadeva or Dharmakirti; not a title of Samudragupta, Kanishka or Harsha.

q: Who was the first ruler who inscribed his messages to his subjects and officials on stone surfaces – natural rocks as well as polished pillars?
explanation: Ashoka was the first ruler to inscribe messages to subjects and officials on natural rocks and polished pillars; Chandragupta Maurya left no edicts and the Guptas came later.

notes.text: - **First Indian ruler to speak directly to his people through inscriptions** – on **natural rocks and polished pillars**, in **Prakrit**: **Ashoka** (APPSC; AP Hostel Welfare Officer) – not Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela, Gautamiputra Satakarni or the Guptas.

exam: APPSC Asst. BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains Paper-II 2017
q: In which rock edict of Asoka, definite mention of the Andhras occur?
explanation: Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras (with the Palidas) among peoples in Ashoka's domain who follow his Dhamma. Ashoka issued only 14 Major Rock Edicts, so a '15th' does not exist.

notes.text: - **Andhras:** the **definite mention of the Andhras** is in **RE XIII** (APPSC Asst. BC & Tribal Welfare Officer 2017 ×2) – listed (with the Palidas) among peoples within Ashoka's domain who follow his Dhamma. There is no 15th RE (only 14).

q: Ashoka used to release certain number of prisoners on humanitarian grounds on every anniversary of his:
explanation: Ashoka released prisoners on every anniversary of his coronation (abhisheka) – 25 releases in 26 years (PE V); not on his birthday, Kalinga or conversion.

notes.text: - **Prisoners:** released on **every anniversary of his coronation (abhisheka)** – 25 releases in 26 years (PE V) (APPSC G1) – not his birth, Kalinga or conversion.

exam: APPSC Assistant Social Welfare, Assistant BC Welfare & Assis
q: In which inscription of Ashoka the Andhras are present?
explanation: The Andhras are named in Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict among the peoples following his Dhamma; there are only 14 Major Rock Edicts.

notes.text: - **Andhras:** the **definite mention of the Andhras** is in **RE XIII** (APPSC Asst. BC & Tribal Welfare Officer 2017 ×2) – listed (with the Palidas) among peoples within Ashoka's domain who follow his Dhamma. There is no 15th RE (only 14).

exam: APPSC Forest Range Officer Mains Paper-I General Studies & M
q: The script used in most of the Ashokan inscriptions was
explanation: Most Ashokan inscriptions are in Prakrit written in Brahmi; Kharosthi was used only in the north-west, and Devanagari and Sharada came much later.

notes.text: - **Script of most edicts:** **Brahmi** (APPSC FRO) – not Devanagari, Kharosthi or Sharada. **Language:** **Prakrit** (State PSC) – not Sanskrit, Pali or Hindi.

q: Which among the following pillar inscriptions of Ashoka states that the land revenue rate of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth?
explanation: The Rummindei (Lumbini) pillar records Ashoka's visit 20 years after consecration, exempting Lumbini from bali and cutting the bhaga to one-eighth. Maski is a rock edict; Kalsi and Vaishali are distractors.

notes.text: - **Lumbini tax cut to 1/8:** **Rummindei pillar** (APPSC G2 2024) – not Maski, Kalsi or Vaishali.

q: Inculcating religious thought in the minds of disciples as the duty of teachers is found in which inscription of Ashoka?
explanation:
Most books and keys: Erragudi. Strictly: Rajula Mandagiri also carries the Minor Rock Edict text on gurus and disciples (AP History APPSC 01 p.11).
The Erragudi (Yerragudi) Minor Rock Edict tells teachers to instil Dhamma in their pupils. Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are not Ashokan edict sites.

notes.text: - **Teachers to inculcate religious thought in disciples:** **Erragudi** (APPSC G2 2008; AP History PYQ) – Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are not Ashokan sites.
- **⚠ Disputed:** most books and keys give **Erragudi**; strictly **Rajula Mandagiri** carries the same Minor RE II text on gurus and disciples (AP History APPSC 01).

q: Which Ashokan inscription states that teachers should inculcate religious thought among disciples?
explanation:
Most books and keys: Erragudi. Strictly: Rajula Mandagiri also carries the Minor Rock Edict text on gurus and disciples (AP History APPSC 01 p.11).
The Erragudi Minor Rock Edict asks teachers to instil Dhamma in their disciples. Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are not Ashokan edict sites.

notes.text: - **Teachers to inculcate religious thought in disciples:** **Erragudi** (APPSC G2 2008; AP History PYQ) – Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are not Ashokan sites.
- **⚠ Disputed:** most books and keys give **Erragudi**; strictly **Rajula Mandagiri** carries the same Minor RE II text on gurus and disciples (AP History APPSC 01).

q: Where are Ashoka's inscriptions found in Andhra Pradesh?
explanation: Ashoka's edicts in Andhra Pradesh are at Erragudi (and Rajula Mandagiri), Kurnool district. Nagarjunakonda, Amaravati and Bhattiprolu are Buddhist sites, not edict sites.

notes.text: - **Ashoka's inscriptions in AP:** **Erragudi** (AP History PYQ) – not Nagarjuna Hill, Amaravati or Bhattiprolu.

q: Which are the earliest inscriptions found in Andhra?
explanation: Ashoka's edicts at Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri (3rd c. BCE) are the earliest inscriptions found in Andhra; Nashik and Hathigumpha are later.

notes.text: - **Earliest inscriptions in Andhra:** **Ashoka's** (AP History PYQ) – in **Prakrit, Brahmi**; they show Mauryan rule reached Rayalaseema. Nashik, Hathigumpha and the Rakshasa caves are later.

q: Kautilya categorizes the Governments and Heads of Departments into 18 tirthas. Amongst these "Dandapala" is the
explanation: Among the 18 tirthas the Dandapala was the chief officer of the army. The treasury was under the Sannidhata and justice under the Pradeshtri and Vyavaharika.

q: Who are the following officers according to Arthasastra was entrusted with the collection of revenue?
explanation: In the Arthashastra the Samaharta was the officer in charge of collecting revenue. The Sannidhata was the treasurer, the Sitadhyaksha the superintendent of crown land and the Samsthadhyaksha of markets.

q: Which Mauryan officer was the incharge of Weights and Measures?
explanation: The Pautavadhyaksha was the superintendent of weights and measures. The Sulkadhyaksha collected tolls, the Samsthadhyaksha supervised markets and the Panyadhyaksha commerce.

exam: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-II Rural Dev
q: In the Mauryan period, the village headman was called?
explanation:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Gramika); it is added as option 5.
The Mauryan village headman was the gramika (Arthashastra), so none of the printed options is right: adhyaksha was a departmental superintendent, and mukhiya, pradhan and sarpanch are later terms.

q:
Consider the following art and architectural forms:
I. Rock-cut elephant at Dhauli in Orissa
II. Yakshi figure from Didarganj near Patna
III. Great Stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh
IV. 80-pillared hall at Kumrahar near Patna
Which of the above art and architectural forms belong to the Mauryan period?
explanation: The Dhauli elephant, the Didarganj Yakshi, the Great Stupa at Sanchi (Ashoka's brick core) and the 80-pillared Kumrahar hall are all Mauryan. Later Sunga additions at Sanchi do not change its Mauryan origin.

notes.text: - **All four Mauryan (APPSC G1):** Dhauli elephant, Didarganj Yakshi, Great Stupa at Sanchi (Ashokan core), 80-pillared hall at Kumrahar.

q: The Mouryan Silver Coin was called
explanation: The Mauryan silver coin was the Pana (karshapana); the Mashaka and Kakani were copper. Niska and Shatamana are older Vedic-era value units.

q: By Mauryan times the main port of the Ganges basin was
explanation: Tamralipti on the east coast was the main port of the Ganga basin in Mauryan times. Sopara and Bharukachchha were west-coast ports and Patala lay in the Indus delta.

q: Which inscription is related to Kharavela?
explanation: The Hathigumpha inscription is Kharavela's. Nasik and Nanaghat are Satavahana records and Amaravati a Buddhist site.

notes.text: - **Hathigumpha inscription** (2nd–1st c. BCE): the year-by-year record of **Kharavela** of Kalinga (UPPSC 2018) – not Ashoka, Harsha or Kanishka; it is not the Girnar, Junagadh or Sarnath inscription.
- **Krishna river = "Kannabenna"** (Kanhabemna) in the Hathigumpha inscription (APPSC AP History).

q: How is the Krishna river referred to in the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela?
explanation: The Hathigumpha inscription calls the Krishna river Kannabenna (Kanhabemna). Kanna and Karna are distractors.

notes.text: - **Krishna river = "Kannabenna"** (Kanhabemna) in the Hathigumpha inscription (APPSC AP History).

q: Which of the following dynasties succeeded the Mauryan Empire in the Deccan region?
explanation: In the Deccan the Mauryas were succeeded by the Satavahanas, former Mauryan feudatories. The Sungas succeeded them in Magadha, and the Kushanas and Guptas came later in the north.

notes.text: - **In the Deccan the Mauryas were succeeded by the Satavahanas** (APPSC ASO) – earlier Mauryan feudatories; founder **Simuka (Srimukha)**; the Puranas call them **Andhra-bhrityas**.

q: Who came to power in Magadha after the Mauryas?
explanation: Pushyamitra Sunga killed the last Maurya Brihadratha and founded the Sunga dynasty in Magadha. The Satavahanas rose in the Deccan, not Magadha.

notes.text: - **Immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha: the Sungas** (APPSC G2 2003, 2008) – not Kushanas, Pandyas or Satavahanas; Sunga dynasty founded **187 BC** (NextGen; PMF: 185 BCE).

q: Who were the immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha ?
explanation: The Sungas founded by Pushyamitra were the immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha. The Satavahanas and Kushanas ruled elsewhere.

notes.text: - **Immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha: the Sungas** (APPSC G2 2003, 2008) – not Kushanas, Pandyas or Satavahanas; Sunga dynasty founded **187 BC** (NextGen; PMF: 185 BCE).

q: Which literature refers to Andhras as ‘Andhakaratta '
explanation: Buddhist (Pali) literature calls the Andhra country Andhakaratta. The Aitareya Brahmana uses 'Andhra'.

q: Which Buddhist text mentions Andhra Path?
explanation: The APPSC 2019 key and NextGen both give the Bhimasena Jataka for 'Andhra Path/Padha'. The Vinayavatthu (printed key) is cited in some lists for 'Andhapatha' but is not the keyed answer, and the Serivanija Jataka names Andhapura.

q: The Buddhist work which refers to Andhra Padha is
explanation: The Bhimasena Jataka refers to Andhra Padha, marking out the Andhra region. The Serivanija Jataka names Andhapura and the Suttanipata the Bavari story.

q: Which literary work mentions the defeat of Kalinga ruler Kharavela by the Asmaka king Satakarni?
explanation: The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka tells of the Asmaka king defeating the king of Kalinga, which the APPSC key reads as Satakarni over Kharavela. Serivanija and Bhimasena Jatakas carry other Andhra references.

q: The Jataka literature which refers to the defeat of Kharavela, the Kalinga king, at the hands of Satakarni, the Asmaka king, was
explanation: The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka is the one cited for the Asmaka victory over Kalinga. The Rajavali-katha is a later Jain work.

q: Which of the following Jatakas mentions 'Dhanyakataka' as 'Andhranagari'?
explanation: The Serivanija Jataka mentions Andhapura (Andhranagari), identified with Dhanyakataka. The Bhimasena Jataka gives Andhra Padha instead.

q: Where did historians find the word 'Andhra', and where did they find the first reference to the Andhras?
explanation: The word 'Andhra' first occurs in the Aitareya Brahmana (Sunahshepa story), naming the Andhras as a people. Buddhist and Jain texts come later.

q: Whose side did the Andhras fight in the Mahabharata war?
explanation: In the Mahabharata the Andhras fought on the Kaurava side. Kichaka was a Matsya commander.

q: Which of the following ancient texts does not mention the Telugu people?
explanation: The Rigveda does not mention the Andhras. The Aitareya Brahmana, the Arthashastra and Kalhana's Rajatarangini do.

q: Which Greek ambassador mentions the Andhras in his treatise?
explanation: Megasthenes, Seleucus' ambassador, mentions the Andhras in his Indica. Pliny and Ptolemy wrote later and were not ambassadors; Marco Polo was a medieval traveller.

q: Assaka is the capital of the people?

q:

explanation: Kujula Kadphises (Kadphises I) founded the Kushana dynasty. Ugrasena (Mathura legend), Vikramaditya and Pushyamitra Shunga are not Kushanas.

q:
Consider the following items:
I. Turban
II. Trousers
III. Heavy long coat
IV. Helmet
V. Boots Which of the items listed above were introduced by the Shakas and Kushans from Central Asia?
options: I, II, III, IV and V
key_text: I, II, III, IV and V
explanation:
The old notes said the APPSC 2024 key leaves out the turban (II–V); the official key could not be found. PMF and R.S. Sharma list the turban first among the Shaka–Kushana items, so all five are keyed.
The Shakas and Kushanas introduced the turban, tunic, trousers and heavy long coat, and Central Asians also brought caps, helmets and boots, so all five items are correct. The old app key (II, III, IV, V) wrongly left out the turban, which the sources list first.

notes.text: - **Dress (Shakas and Kushanas):** **turban, tunic, trousers and heavy long coat** (the sherwani descends from the coat); Central Asians also brought **caps, helmets and boots** → all five items, **I, II, III, IV and V** (APPSC G1 PYQ).

q: What is Amaravati famous for?

q: Sthapathi means
explanation: In the Agama-Shilpa tradition the sthapati is the master craftsman-architect who designs and directs the making of temples and images, i.e. the master who makes sculptures. The carver working under him is the shilpi, and the vardhaki and takshaka are the builders and carvers; a chief purohit is a priest.

notes.text: - **Sthapati (temple tradition):** the **master craftsman-architect** who designs and directs the making of temples and images – "the master who makes sculptures" (APPSC Endowment 2022); the carver under him is the **shilpi**, the builders and carvers under him the **vardhaki** and **takshaka**.

q: Who among the following is recognized as the founder of Satavahana rule?
explanation: Simukha (Srimukha) founded Satavahana rule; Satakarni I, Kuntala Satakarni and Gautamiputra Satakarni were later kings.

q: Under whom did the Andhras gain independence from Mauryan rule?
explanation: The Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories, and the Andhras won freedom from the Mauryas under them, with Srimukha (Simuka) as the first king.

q: The Satavahana kings who ruled Andhra belonged to which caste?
explanation: The Satavahanas are regarded as Brahmins: the Nasik inscription calls Gautamiputra Satakarni 'Ekabrahmana'.

q: The oldest of the Deccan rulers?
explanation: The Satavahanas (c. 200 BC – 200 AD) are the oldest Deccan dynasty; the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Cholas are later.

q: The first dynasty which ruled Andhra was:
explanation: The Satavahanas were the first major dynasty to rule Andhra; the Cholas, Eastern Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas came later.

q: The first dynasty to rule Andhra?
explanation: The Satavahanas were the first major dynasty to rule Andhra.

They had matrimonial alliance with Kakatiyas
key_text: They had matrimonial alliance with Kakatiyas
explanation: The Satavahanas (c. 1st c. BCE-3rd c. CE) could not have had marriage ties with the Kakatiyas (12th-14th c.); they are called Andhrabhrityas in the Puranas, issued bilingual Prakrit-Tamil coins and patronised both Buddhism and Vedic religion.

q: Whom did Gautamiputra Satakarni have to face?
explanation: Gautamiputra Satakarni fought the Sakas (the Kshaharata Nahapana) and is called the 'destroyer of the Sakas'.

q: The Satavahanas regained their lost territories from Nahapana during the reign of which king?
explanation: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana and regained Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan and Nasik.

q: Which inscription describes the military victories of Gautamiputra Satakarni?
explanation: Gautami Balasri's Nasik inscription (prasasti) describes the achievements and victories of her son Gautamiputra Satakarni. Naneghat belongs to Naganika (Satakarni I), Kodavali to Chanda Satakarni and Hathigumpha to Kharavela.

q: What was the name of the capital of 'Anupa', ruled by Gautamiputra Satakarni?
explanation: Anupa, named among Gautamiputra's regions in the Nasik Prasasti, was the Narmada valley, with its capital at Mahishmati. Vidisha and Ujjain belong to Akara and Avanti.
